title: "Specialized Iterator Traits"

# Specialized Iterator Traits

`Iterator` is the minimum. A few marker and extension traits tell consumers they may start from the back, look ahead, trust the length, or assume that `None` is permanent.

## The concept

| Trait | Extra promise |
|-------|----------------|
| `DoubleEndedIterator` | `next_back` yields from the end, and it meets `next` in the middle |
| `ExactSizeIterator` | `len` is the exact number of remaining items |
| `FusedIterator` | After `None`, every later `next` is `None` |
| `Peekable` | Not a trait you implement. An adaptor that can look at the next item without taking it |

Implement these only when the promise is true. A wrong `len` is a logic bug. A type that claims `FusedIterator` and then yields `Some` after `None` breaks consumers that stop checking.

## Recipe 44 — Iterating in reverse with DoubleEndedIterator

Slices, ranges, and `Vec` iterators are double-ended.

```rust
fn main() {
    let names = ["ada", "linus", "grace"];
    let mut iter = names.iter();
    assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some(&"ada"));
    assert_eq!(iter.next_back(), Some(&"grace"));
    assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some(&"linus"));
    assert_eq!(iter.next_back(), None);

    let reversed: Vec<_> = names.iter().rev().copied().collect();
    assert_eq!(reversed, ["grace", "linus", "ada"]);
}
```

`rev` needs `DoubleEndedIterator`. It swaps `next` and `next_back`. `next` and `next_back` on the same iterator share one cursor pair, so they do not repeat items.

## Recipe 45 — Implementing DoubleEndedIterator for a custom type

A countdown that can also count up from the low end.

```rust
struct Span {
    start: i32,
    end: i32,
}

impl Iterator for Span {
    type Item = i32;

    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> {
        if self.start >= self.end {
            return None;
        }
        let n = self.start;
        self.start += 1;
        Some(n)
    }
}

impl DoubleEndedIterator for Span {
    fn next_back(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> {
        if self.start >= self.end {
            return None;
        }
        self.end -= 1;
        Some(self.end)
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut span = Span { start: 1, end: 5 };
    assert_eq!(span.next(), Some(1));
    assert_eq!(span.next_back(), Some(4));
    let rest: Vec<_> = span.collect();
    assert_eq!(rest, [2, 3]);

    let backwards: Vec<_> = Span { start: 0, end: 3 }.rev().collect();
    assert_eq!(backwards, [2, 1, 0]);
}
```

`end` is exclusive, matching `start..end`. Both methods must agree on the empty condition `start >= end`.

## Recipe 46 — Peeking at the next element without consuming it

`peekable` clones the look-ahead as an `Option` sitting in the adaptor. `peek` returns `Option<&Item>`. `next` returns that item and refills.

```rust
fn main() {
    let readings = [10, 10, 12, 12, 12, 15];
    let mut iter = readings.into_iter().peekable();
    let mut runs = Vec::new();

    while let Some(value) = iter.next() {
        let mut count = 1;
        while iter.peek() == Some(&value) {
            iter.next();
            count += 1;
        }
        runs.push((value, count));
    }

    assert_eq!(runs, [(10, 2), (12, 3), (15, 1)]);
}
```

`peek` borrows the iterator. You cannot call `next` while that borrow is held. The `while` condition ends the borrow before the body calls `next`, which is why this compiles.

This groups consecutive equals. It does not sort. A lone `15` after a gap is its own run.

## Recipe 47 — Implementing FusedIterator for correctness

A fused iterator that has returned `None` keeps returning `None`. Some hand-written iterators are not fused: they can yield `Some` again. `fuse` wraps those and suppresses later items.

```rust
struct Blip {
    phase: u8,
}

impl Iterator for Blip {
    type Item = &'static str;

    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> {
        self.phase += 1;
        match self.phase {
            1 => Some("on"),
            2 => None,
            3 => Some("again"),
            _ => None,
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut raw = Blip { phase: 0 };
    assert_eq!(raw.next(), Some("on"));
    assert_eq!(raw.next(), None);
    assert_eq!(raw.next(), Some("again"));

    let mut fused = Blip { phase: 0 }.fuse();
    assert_eq!(fused.next(), Some("on"));
    assert_eq!(fused.next(), None);
    assert_eq!(fused.next(), None);
}
```

`fuse` is the adaptor. `FusedIterator` is the marker you implement when your own `next` already has that property, so callers do not need a second flag.

```rust
struct OnceThenDone {
    value: Option<i32>,
}

impl Iterator for OnceThenDone {
    type Item = i32;

    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> {
        self.value.take()
    }
}

impl std::iter::FusedIterator for OnceThenDone {}

fn main() {
    let mut iter = OnceThenDone { value: Some(7) };
    assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some(7));
    assert_eq!(iter.next(), None);
    assert_eq!(iter.next(), None);
}
```

The empty `impl FusedIterator` says "I promise". The compiler does not check the promise. `Option::take` makes the promise true here.

## Recipe 48 — Using size_hint() and len() downstream

`ExactSizeIterator::len` is the remaining count. Slice iterators implement it. A `for` loop does not need it. `collect` and `zip` can use the hint to allocate or to stop.

```rust
fn main() {
    let names = ["ada", "linus", "grace"];
    let iter = names.iter();
    assert_eq!(iter.len(), 3);
    assert_eq!(iter.size_hint(), (3, Some(3)));

    let mut iter = iter;
    iter.next();
    assert_eq!(iter.len(), 2);
}
```

`len` consumes nothing. It is not `count`, which would take the items.

When you implement `ExactSizeIterator`, also implement `size_hint` so both agree. `len` has a default that reads `size_hint` and expects the lower and upper bounds to match.

```rust
struct Countdown {
    left: u32,
}

impl Iterator for Countdown {
    type Item = u32;

    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> {
        self.left = self.left.checked_sub(1)?;
        Some(self.left)
    }

    fn size_hint(&self) -> (usize, Option<usize>) {
        (self.left as usize, Some(self.left as usize))
    }
}

impl ExactSizeIterator for Countdown {}

fn main() {
    let ticks = Countdown { left: 3 };
    assert_eq!(ticks.len(), 3);
    let values: Vec<_> = ticks.collect();
    assert_eq!(values, [2, 1, 0]);
}
```

`len` is 3 and three items come out. The yielded values are the numbers after each decrement, so a countdown that starts with `left == 3` produces `2, 1, 0`.
